title: Primary hypothyroidism (adult)
subject: endocrinology
summary: Confirm with TSH then FT4, start levothyroxine 1.6 mcg/kg/day in adults under 65 without heart disease (25 to 50 mcg/day if older or cardiac), keep TSH within the reference range, recheck 4 to 6 weeks after each dose change, and raise the dose 20 to 30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.

sections.title: Recognise and define
items: Symptoms are non-specific: fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, hoarse voice, menstrual change, low mood, slow-relaxing reflexes. One symptom alone rarely indicates thyroid disease.

Overt primary hypothyroidism: TSH above the reference range with low FT4. Subclinical hypothyroidism: raised TSH with normal FT4. Central hypothyroidism (pituitary or hypothalamic disease): low FT4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH.

Offer testing with type 1 diabetes or other autoimmune disease and with new atrial fibrillation; consider it in depression or unexplained anxiety. Do not test solely because a person has type 2 diabetes (NICE).
Common causes: autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis, previous radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy, drugs (amiodarone, lithium, immune checkpoint inhibitors, antithyroid drugs) and iodine deficiency.
Hypothyroidism with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, hyponatraemia or reduced consciousness is myxoedema coma: see the myxoedema coma protocol.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Measure TSH first; if it is above the range, measure FT4 on the same sample. Measure TSH and FT4 together when pituitary disease is suspected.
Do not test during an acute illness unless thyroid disease is the suspected cause: non-thyroidal illness distorts results. Do not repeat tests sooner than 6 weeks.
Measure thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPOAb) once when TSH is raised (positive antibodies predict progression); do not repeat TPOAb.
Suspected adrenal insufficiency or hypopituitarism: exclude or treat adrenal insufficiency (hydrocortisone first) before starting levothyroxine, which can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Biotin supplements and assay interference can produce misleading results; suspect this when TSH and FT4 do not fit the clinical picture.

sections.title: Levothyroxine: start and titrate
items: Offer levothyroxine (LT4) as first-line treatment. Do not routinely offer liothyronine (alone or combined with LT4) or natural thyroid extract (NICE, ATA).
Adults under 65 without cardiovascular disease: start 1.6 mcg/kg/day rounded to the nearest 25 mcg (for example 100 mcg/day for a 60 kg adult).
Age 65 or over, or cardiovascular disease: start 25 to 50 mcg/day and titrate. Known coronary artery disease: start 12.5 to 25 mcg/day and increase slowly, watching for angina or arrhythmia.
Mild disease (TSH 10 mIU/L or less, or subclinical): lower doses such as 25 to 50 mcg/day are usually enough (ATA).
Adjust in steps of 12.5 to 25 mcg/day according to TSH, rechecking 4 to 6 weeks after any change (time to steady state).
Take on an empty stomach, consistently, either 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime 3 or more hours after the evening meal. Separate from calcium, iron, antacids and sucralfate by about 4 hours.

Requirements change with weight change, ageing, pregnancy, malabsorption (coeliac disease, gastritis, bariatric surgery), nephrotic syndrome and interacting drugs; no adjustment is needed for renal or liver failure alone.

sections.title: Subclinical hypothyroidism
items: Confirm on 2 occasions 3 months apart: about half of TSH values of 5 to 10 mIU/L return to normal without treatment (NICE).
TSH 10 mIU/L or higher on 2 occasions 3 months apart: consider levothyroxine and monitor as for overt disease.
TSH above the range but below 10 mIU/L with symptoms, age under 65: consider a 6-month trial of levothyroxine; if symptoms persist once TSH is in range, consider stopping.
TSH rises with age (97.5th centile about 7.5 mIU/L in healthy older people); mild elevation in the very old is often physiological and rarely needs treatment.
Untreated or stopped: check TSH and FT4 yearly if TPOAb positive or after thyroid surgery or radioiodine, otherwise every 2 to 3 years (NICE).

sections.title: Targets and monitoring
items: Aim for TSH within the reference range (typically about 0.5 to 4 mIU/L). Avoid doses that lower TSH below the range, especially below 0.1 mIU/L: atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis risk in older people and postmenopausal women.
After starting or changing the dose, recheck TSH in 4 to 6 weeks (ATA) or within 3 months (NICE); once 2 similar values are in range, check yearly.
Very high baseline TSH or long-standing disease: TSH can take up to 6 months to normalise, so avoid over-titrating early.
Over 70 to 80 years, a TSH target of 4 to 6 mIU/L is reasonable (ATA).
Persistent symptoms with an in-range TSH: check adherence and timing of doses, measure FT4, and look for other causes before increasing the dose.
Central hypothyroidism: monitor FT4, not TSH.

sections.title: Pregnancy and planning pregnancy
items: Women on levothyroxine planning pregnancy: aim for TSH below 2.5 mIU/L before conception and test promptly once pregnant.
As soon as pregnancy is confirmed, increase the dose by 20 to 30%, for example by taking 2 extra daily doses each week (9 doses per week), and inform the clinician.
Check TSH about every 4 weeks until mid-gestation and again later in pregnancy (around 30 weeks); keep it within the trimester-specific reference range used by the local laboratory.
Overt hypothyroidism found in pregnancy: start full replacement promptly; untreated disease increases miscarriage, hypertension, preterm birth and impaired fetal neurodevelopment.
After delivery, return to the pre-pregnancy dose and check TSH about 6 weeks postpartum.
Euthyroid women with positive TPOAb: levothyroxine does not improve fertility or reduce miscarriage or preterm birth (ATA 2026); monitor TSH instead.

sections.title: Refer to endocrinology
items: Pregnancy, or planning pregnancy, with thyroid disease.
Central hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism or suspected adrenal insufficiency.
Cardiac disease limiting titration, drug-induced disease (amiodarone, lithium, checkpoint inhibitors), discordant or unusual results, or symptoms persisting despite an in-range TSH.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating a single raised TSH, or a TSH measured during acute illness or recovery from it.
Chasing symptoms with doses that suppress TSH, causing iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis, atrial fibrillation and bone loss.
Levothyroxine taken with breakfast, coffee, calcium or iron causing erratic TSH; check how it is taken before increasing the dose.
Starting full-dose levothyroxine in an older patient with ischaemic heart disease.
Forgetting the pregnancy dose increase, or not returning to the pre-pregnancy dose after delivery.

drugs.name: Levothyroxine (adult under 65, no heart disease)
drugs.dose: 1.6 mcg/kg/day orally once daily, rounded to the nearest 25 mcg
drugs.notes: Titrate by 12.5 to 25 mcg/day every 4 to 6 weeks to a TSH in the reference range. Empty stomach, 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime.

drugs.name: Levothyroxine (65 or over, or cardiovascular disease)
drugs.dose: 25 to 50 mcg/day orally; 12.5 to 25 mcg/day in known coronary artery disease
drugs.notes: Increase slowly; watch for angina and arrhythmia. Target TSH 4 to 6 mIU/L may be acceptable over 70 to 80 years.

drugs.name: Levothyroxine (pregnancy adjustment)
drugs.dose: Increase the pre-pregnancy dose by 20 to 30% on confirmation of pregnancy (2 extra daily doses per week)
drugs.notes: TSH every 4 weeks to mid-gestation; return to the pre-pregnancy dose after delivery.
